stories.title: How do you measure a rupee?
stories.covers: Three ways to measure the rupee and the question each answers.
stories.shows: ₹ per $ since 2004; 40-currency NEER and REER (2015-16 = 100)
stories.oneLine: A dollar costs more than twice as many rupees as in 2004, yet Indian goods cost buyers abroad about what they did then. Three ways to measure the rupee, and the question each answers.
stories.briefHtml:
Live on dev · /rupee-and-world · 09-10-2026 · PR #38; CEO review PR #47Owner: VishesWave 1The rupee and the worldEffort: large

The rupee went from ₹46 to ₹88 a dollar in 22 years and made headlines at every step. Measured against 40 trading partners and adjusted for prices, it ended within a point of where it started. Both numbers are true; they answer different questions.

₹45.95 → ₹88.31
rupees per US dollar, yearly average, 2003-04 to 2025-26 exchange rates FY
−44%
nominal effective rate (40 currencies, trade weights), Apr 2004 → Jul 2026: 138.5 → 78.0 REER/NEER monthly
90.9 → 91.8
real effective rate over the same months, base 2015-16 = 100 REER/NEER monthly
≈108 → ≈91
real rate, Nov 2024 peak to mid-2026: a bigger swing in 20 months than across 22 years Drishti, 04-08-2026

Narrative

  1. Guess. "Since 2004 a dollar went from ₹46 to ₹88. How much did the price of Indian goods change for buyers abroad?" A slider from 0 to 60%.
  2. The dollar line. Rupees per dollar, and the 40-currency nominal index, down 44%.
  3. The turn. Prices rose faster in India than in its partners. Adjust for that and the real index is flat: 90.9 then, 91.8 now.
  4. The swings that do matter. The real rate climbs to about 108 in late 2024, then drops to about 89–92 by 2026. Short swings, not the long slide, move competitiveness.
  5. "Record low" and "undervalued" can both be true. 2026 is the example. Close with what each number answers.

For the reader

  • Why the rupee–dollar rate mostly reflects price differences between countries.
  • What the headline "record low" does and does not tell you.
  • A personal hook: what a $1,000 course fee cost in 2004 and today, and in "real" terms.

For economists

  • The decomposition, live: real change ≈ nominal change + India's inflation − partners' inflation, by year.
  • Toggles: 6- versus 40-currency basket; trade versus export weights; monthly versus annual average.
  • The base issue stated plainly: 100 means parity with 2015-16, not equilibrium.
  • Series codes, the January 2021 rebasing note, and CSVs.

Where readers play

Toggle nominal / realScrub 2004 → 2026Basket: 6 or 40 currenciesFee calculator (fixed inputs)
What economists and institutions are saying 2017 to 2026
  • The real rate peaked at about 108 in November 2024, read then as about 8% overvalued against 2015-16, and fell below 100 by mid-2025 ThePrint, 07-10-2025.
  • Governor Malhotra: "We don't target any specific price levels or bands" (05-12-2025, rupee near 90) BS. A late-July 2026 remark calling the rupee undervalued is reported only secondhand so far.
  • IMF's 2025 Article IV reclassified India's de facto regime from "stabilised" to "crawl-like" IMF, 24-11-2025.
  • 2026: the rupee crossed 95 on 30-04-2026 after the Hormuz disruption; RBI's June measures included an FCNR(B) hedging subsidy; the swap window drew $52.3 billion before early closure RBI BT, 14-08-2026.
  • Raghuram Rajan, January 2025: the slide was "really a dollar issue" BT. Arvind Subramanian argued in 2017 that an overvalued rupee hurt competitiveness BS.
  • Gap worth filling: no interactive piece shows the dollar rate, NEER and REER together from 2004.
Fact-check traps 7 items
  • RBI rebased in January 2021: 2004-05 → 2015-16 base, 36 → 40 currencies, back-cast to 2004-05 only RBI Bulletin. Do not splice to the 1993 series.
  • REER of 100 is parity with 2015-16, not "fair value". Never write "overvalued by X%" without "relative to 2015-16".
  • Current REER is CPI-based; older debates used WPI-based measures.
  • Recent months are provisional; outlets quote 108.03 to 109.86 for the same peak. Pin the vintage.
  • Percent direction: ₹45.95 → ₹88.31 is a 92% rise in rupees per dollar and a 48% fall in the rupee's dollar value. Pick one convention.
  • FY2025-26 average is ₹88.31; the 2026 spot rate went past 96. Say which.
  • "Crawl-like", not "crawling peg", and the IMF says the label is statistical and backward-looking.

stories.title: What ₹1 lakh could buy
stories.covers: What ₹1 lakh bought each year from 2001 to 2026, and what it is worth today.
stories.shows: Gold and silver prices; mason's wage; ₹ per $; wheat MSP; CPI-IW chained
stories.oneLine: One sum, carried from 2001 to 2026: what it bought each year in gold, silver, a mason's days, dollars and wheat, and what it is worth today.
stories.briefHtml:
Live on dev · /what-one-lakh-bought · 09-10-2026 · PR #40Owner: GeetikaWave 1 · flagshipMoney and paymentsEffort: medium

Your parents' ₹1 lakh and yours are not the same money. This story takes one sum through 25 years and shows what it bought each year in gold, silver, a mason's days, dollars and wheat, and what it is worth today. Then it asks which of those changed most, and why that matters for anyone saving.

224 g → 6.7 g
gold bought by ₹1 lakh, 2001 → 2026 (Jan–Jul average) gold and silver prices
₹4.38 lakh
what ₹1 lakh of 2001 is worth in 2026 prices CPI industrial workers
913 → 153
days of a rural mason's work ₹1 lakh paid for, 2001 → 2025 wage rates
$2,097 → $1,132
dollars ₹1 lakh bought, 2001-02 → 2025-26 exchange rates FY

Narrative

  1. The heirloom. "In 2001 your family had ₹1 lakh for a wedding. What could it buy in gold?" Reader picks from necklace, bangles, chain, ring. Reveal: about 224 grams, a heavy necklace set.
  2. Ten years on. The same ₹1 lakh in 2011: 42 grams. The necklace shrinks on screen to bangles. 2021: a chain. 2026: a ring.
  3. Prices rose too. ₹1 lakh of 2001 is worth ₹4.38 lakh today. Bring that back to gold and the necklace still would not come back: it would need ₹33.6 lakh.
  4. The other shelves. A mason's days, dollars, wheat. Each shrinks at its own pace. The reader sees that "inflation" is not one number: gold ran ahead, labour ran ahead of prices, the dollar moved in steps, wheat support prices kept pace.
  5. Your own year. The reader enters any year and amount, from ₹10,000 to ₹10 lakh, and gets their own shelf, with a link to share it.

For the reader

  • Inflation made physical: the shrinking necklace.
  • Why "₹1 lakh was a lot of money" was true, and by how much.
  • A shareable card for their own year and amount.

For economists

  • Relative prices made visible: gold, labour, the dollar and food against one general index.
  • The deflator is named and chained, with the linking factors shown; a toggle swaps CPI-IW for the farm-labourer index or WPI.
  • Real returns on gold over any window, as a by-product.

Where readers play

Pick a yearPick an amountSwap the yardstickShrinking necklace (guided)
Fact-check traps 5 items
  • CPI-IW chaining uses the Labour Bureau's linking factors (4.63 for 1982 → 2001, 2.88 for 2001 → 2016). Confirm both from the Labour Bureau's own notes in gate 2.
  • Gold is the Mumbai monthly average, not a jeweller's price; 2026 is a part-year average and gold fell from its March 2026 peak.
  • The mason series is one occupation and one gender; the Labour Bureau's occupation codes changed in November 2013 (this series runs through it, but check the definition).
  • Support prices are matched to the year by marketing year; state that alignment.
  • Object names (necklace, bangles) need cited typical weights, or the reader chooses the object.

stories.title: The phone pays, but the cash stays
stories.covers: Digital payments multiplied while cash in circulation kept growing.
stories.shows: UPI, ATM and micro-ATM volumes since Nov 2019; currency in circulation; note denominations
stories.oneLine: UPI payments grew 19.4 times between November 2019 and July 2026. Over the ten years to March 2026, currency in circulation grew 2.5 times.
stories.briefHtml:
Live on dev · /the-phone-pays-the-cash-stays · 12-10-2026 · PR #42Owner: VishesWave 1Money and paymentsEffort: large

UPI payments grew nineteen-fold in under seven years and ATM withdrawals fell by a third. Cash in circulation rose to ₹41.7 lakh crore. People changed how they pay. They did not change how much cash they keep.

122 → 2,366crore
UPI payments a month, Nov 2019 → Jul 2026 payment system indicators
62.7 → 40.8crore
ATM cash withdrawals a month, same months payment system indicators
3.4 → 9.7crore
micro-ATM withdrawals a month (village banking agents) payment system indicators
₹16.6 → ₹41.7lakh cr
currency in circulation, Mar 2016 → Mar 2026 reserve money components

Narrative

  1. Guess. "UPI now handles over 2,000 crore payments a month. Since 2016, has the cash people hold gone up or down?"
  2. November 2016. November 2016: ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes, 86% of the value of cash, withdrawn. Cash falls to 8.7% of GDP.
  3. UPI grows. UPI payments multiply. Debit-card payments fall from 41.8 to 10.2 crore a month: UPI's first replacement was the card, not the note.
  4. Cash returns to its earlier share. Cash held climbs back to around its pre-2016 share. ATM withdrawals fall. People hold notes and spend them less.
  5. Where cash moves. Micro-ATM withdrawals at village banking agents rise from 3.4 to 9.7 crore a month. Close on the stock-versus-flow distinction, the core of the story.

For the reader

  • The answer to "if everyone uses UPI, why is there more cash?": paying and keeping are different jobs.
  • What happened to the ₹2,000 note, in one scene.
  • A "your monthly cash" comparison: average ATM withdrawal rose from about ₹4,500 to about ₹5,400.

For economists

  • Transaction demand against store-of-value and precautionary demand, as in RBI's own research RBI Occasional Paper RBI Bulletin, 24-09-2025.
  • Toggles: CIC or currency with the public; GDP base; March or average-of-year.
  • The global cash paradox for context ECB 2021 BIS 2018.

Where readers play

Crore / index toggleDenomination wall, year by yearScrub cash to GDP 1971 → 2026Payments scene (fixed)
What economists and institutions are saying
  • RBI researchers find currency demand driven by "precautionary and store-of-value motives" while "use of cash as a payment medium continues to fall"; cash-to-GDP peaked at 14.4% in 2020-21, inflated by pandemic GDP RBI.
  • RBI Bulletin, September 2025: UPI is negatively associated with cash demand, but income dominates; the authors say the estimates "do not necessarily imply causality" RBI.
  • RBI Annual Report 2025-26: banknotes in circulation up 11.9% in value to ₹41,23,995 crore (notes only); ₹500 notes about 85.5% of value; e₹ ₹771.7 crore, down on the year RBI AR.
  • SBI Research: 86% of UPI merchant payments are under ₹500, so UPI competes with small notes Moneylife, 16-02-2026.
  • 98.45% of ₹2,000 notes had returned by 31-03-2026 Angel One.
Fact-check traps 6 items
  • GDP base. MoSPI moved to a 2022-23 base on 27-02-2026, lowering nominal GDP by about 3–4% PIB. Our 11.7% uses the old base; on the new base it is likely nearer 12%. The back series is due by December 2026. Decision wait for it, or publish on the old base with a stated note.
  • Currency in circulation includes cash held by banks; currency with the public excludes it. Name the series.
  • March 2017 is a remonetisation trough, not an equilibrium. Festival and election months spike.
  • Card and ATM data before November 2019 are not comparable. Never splice.
  • Do not compare a monthly UPI value (a flow) with the cash stock.
  • P2P transfers are 71% of UPI value; much of UPI is people moving money, not spending that replaces cash.

stories.title: Money in, money out
stories.covers: Money Indians abroad send home, keep in Indian banks, and what residents send abroad.
stories.shows: Private transfers since 1950-51; NRI deposits; LRS outflows by purpose; gross FDI
stories.oneLine: Indians abroad sent home $135.4 billion in 2024-25 and keep $165.7 billion in Indian banks; Indians at home sent $29.6 billion abroad, more than half of it for travel.
stories.briefHtml:
Live on dev · /money-in-money-out · 13-10-2026 · PR #50Owner: VishesWave 2The rupee and the worldEffort: medium

In 1990-91 Indians abroad sent home $2.1 billion. In 2024-25 the figure was $135.4 billion, more than India received in gross foreign direct investment. Meanwhile, a new outbound middle class now sends about $30 billion a year the other way, more than half of it for travel.

$2.1 → $135.4bn
private transfer receipts, 1990-91 → 2024-25 invisibles by category
$118.7 > $71.0bn
private transfers against gross FDI inflows, 2023-24 invisibles foreign investment
$1.3 → $29.6bn
outward remittances under LRS, 2014-15 → 2024-25 (peak $31.7 bn in 2023-24) outward remittance
$17.0bn
of 2024-25 LRS went on travel; study abroad peaked at $5.0 bn in 2019-20 outward remittance

Narrative

  1. Guess. "Which brings more foreign money into India each year: foreign companies investing, or Indians abroad sending money home?"
  2. The stream swells. From $2.1 billion in 1990-91 to $135 billion. The senders change too: advanced economies now supply about half, the Gulf about 38% RBI survey, 19-03-2025.
  3. The steady one. Year to year, money sent home moves far less than portfolio or FDI flows.
  4. The new stream. LRS outflows: travel, gifts, support for relatives, study, investment. The October 2023 change to tax collected at source shows as a rise before and a fall after.
  5. The balance. For every ₹100 that comes home, about ₹22 now goes out under LRS.

For the reader

  • The size of the diaspora economy, in a unit they can feel.
  • Where their own foreign travel and fees show up in national data.
  • A clear answer to "is it still the Gulf?".

For economists

  • Volatility comparison: remittances against FDI and portfolio flows.
  • Remittances against the merchandise trade deficit (about 42% financed on average, 2010-11 to 2023-24, per RBI).
  • LRS as a liberalisation record with clear policy breaks: ceiling changes, TCS, the credit-card carve-out.

Where readers play

Scrub 1971 → 2025Filter LRS by purpose₹100 in, ₹ outSource-country map (fixed)
Live debates
  • India was the top recipient in calendar 2024 at about $129 billion (World Bank) BS, 18-12-2024.
  • RBI's Sixth Remittances Survey: the US share rose to 27.7% in 2023-24; Maharashtra receives 20.5% and Kerala 19.7%; sending $200 cost 4.9% RBI.
  • Whether India's remittances are countercyclical is disputed in the literature 2021 study.
  • Indian students abroad fell from about 13.3 lakh (2024) to about 12.5 lakh (2025) ICEF.
Fact-check traps 5 items
  • Private transfers are not only remittances. The line includes local withdrawals from NRI deposits and other items. Use "money sent home" only for the remittance component, or name the measure exactly. Check whether RBI now publishes workers' remittances separately.
  • RBI reports April–March; the World Bank reports calendar years. Do not mix them in a ranking.
  • LRS travel understates foreign travel spend: overseas credit-card use sits outside LRS.
  • LRS categories before 2015-16 are incomplete (travel and study start near zero); begin purpose charts in 2015-16.
  • Our bulletin LRS file is mislabelled (total at index 9). Use the SDMX series until it is fixed.

stories.title: The 10-gram question
stories.covers: Why 10 grams of gold cost 42 times its 1990 price: the dollar price, the rupee and Mumbai's premium.
stories.shows: Mumbai gold since 1990; dollar gold price; ₹ per $; gold in forex reserves
stories.oneLine: Ten grams of gold cost about 42 times as many rupees as in 1990: how much is the dollar price of gold, how much the rupee, and how much the gap between the world price and Mumbai's.
stories.briefHtml:
Live on dev · /the-10-gram-question · 14-10-2026 · PR #51Owner: GeetikaWave 2The rupee and the worldEffort: medium

Ten grams of gold cost ₹3,417 in Mumbai in April 1990 and ₹1,42,606 in July 2026. Part of that rise is the dollar price of gold, part is the rupee–dollar rate, and part is import duty. The RBI's own gold went from 5.5% of India's reserves to 14.5%, mostly through price.

42×
Mumbai gold, Apr 1990 → Jul 2026, about 10.8% a year gold and silver prices
≈8×
faster than the workers' price index since 2001 (gold ×33.6, CPI-IW ×4.4) Our reading
5.5% → 14.5%
gold's share of forex reserves, Dec 2016 → Sep 2026 ($20 bn → $111 bn) forex reserves weekly
6% → 15%
import duty, cut in July 2024 and raised again from 13-05-2026 The Week

Narrative

  1. The wedding year. Pick a year and a sum; see the jewellery it bought.
  2. The shrinking necklace. The same sum, year by year, down to a ring.
  3. Three engines. Split the rupee price of gold into the dollar gold price, the rupee's fall (from S6) and import duty. This is the economist's decomposition, drawn as three stacked bars per decade.
  4. Against a fixed deposit. The race, with interest rates from DBIE.
  5. The country's gold. The RBI's share of reserves rose mostly through price; tonnes moved little. Close without advice: what the past did, not what to buy.

For the reader

  • The family-jewellery question, answered with their own year.
  • Why Indian gold costs more than Dubai's: duty and the rupee.
  • What the RBI's gold is and why its share grew.

For economists

  • ₹ gold return ≈ $ gold return + rupee depreciation + duty change, by window.
  • Real return against CPI and against fixed-deposit rates, any start year.
  • Valuation against volume in the reserves.

Where readers play

Your year and amountReal / nominalRace start yearDecomposition (fixed per decade)
Live debates
  • Household gold estimates range from WGC's dated 25,000 t to Morgan Stanley's 34,600 t (June 2025) BS. Treat as a range.
  • Sovereign Gold Bonds stopped after February 2024; the gold monetisation scheme's medium and long-term deposits ended 26-03-2025.
  • RBI held 880.52 t at end-March 2026 and brought 104 t home in the half-year to March RBI.
  • The organised gold-loan book is put at about ₹18 lakh crore (ICRA, July 2026); new loan-to-value rules apply from 01-04-2026.
Fact-check traps 5 items
  • Mumbai price is not international price × exchange rate: duty, GST and premiums sit between.
  • Check purity (999 or 995) and whether DBIE's figure is an average or month-end. Our July 2026 figure is below some trade quotes for the same month.
  • Mark both duty changes on any premium chart.
  • Reserve share rising is a valuation effect; say tonnes alongside.
  • No advice. "Gold beat fixed deposits from year X" is history; "buy gold" is not ours to say.

stories.title: What households keep
stories.covers: Merged into S18 as its saving-and-borrowing chapter.
stories.shows: Household gross financial saving, borrowing and net saving as % of GDP; instrument mix
stories.oneLine: Households did not save less; they borrowed more, and the new data shows that easing.
stories.briefHtml:
Merged into S18 on 14-10-2026Wave 2HouseholdsEffort: mediumBlocked on data base

Merged into S18. This plan is now S18's saving-and-borrowing chapter; the plan below is kept for its research and traps. The 2022-23 base it waited for is in Handbook table 245 (totals only).

"Indians are saving less" was a 2023 headline. The data says something more precise: households kept putting about the same share of income into financial assets, and borrowed more against it. The newest official estimates, on the 2022-23 base, show borrowing easing again in 2024-25.

3.8% → 6.2%
household borrowing, % of GDP, 2021-22 → 2023-24 (old base) household flows
≈11–12%
gross financial saving, % of GDP, roughly flat across the decade (old base) sector-wise savings
5.2 → 7.0%
net financial saving, % of GNDI, 2022-23 → 2024-25 on the new base RBI AR 2025-26
₹45 per ₹100
into mutual funds and shares for every ₹100 into deposits, 2024-25 (₹21 in 2020-21) BS, 27-11-2025

Narrative

  1. Guess. "Out of every ₹100 a household earns, how much ends up as net financial savings?"
  2. Two sides of one ledger. What goes in (deposits, insurance, PF, funds, shares, cash) and what is borrowed (homes, vehicles, personal loans).
  3. The 2023 headline, unpacked. Gross saving flat; borrowing up; so net saving down. Arithmetic, not a judgement.
  4. The mix moves. From deposits towards mutual funds and shares; from banks towards NBFCs as lenders.
  5. The newer picture. On the new base, borrowing eases in 2024-25. End on why we date every number: the story depended on the vintage.

For the reader

  • A straight answer to "are Indians saving less?".
  • Where the family rupee goes, compared with their own.
  • Why headlines said 47-year low and 50-year low at once.

For economists

  • Vintage toggle: the same year as first estimated and as revised.
  • Old base against new base, side by side, never spliced.
  • Stock (debt-to-GDP, about 41–45%) and flow (borrowing about 5–6%) on separate, labelled panels.
  • GDP against GNDI denominators.

Where readers play

Scrub yearsYour household splitVintage toggleInstrument tap (fixed values)
Live debates
  • September 2023: RBI data put net financial saving at 5.1% of GDP for 2022-23, the lowest since 1975-76; the Finance Ministry said there was "no distress" and that borrowing went to homes and vehicles BS, 21-09-2023.
  • SBI Research called the low-savings reading "completely misleading", citing physical savings BS. Motilal Oswal's Nikhil Gupta read rising non-housing debt as a concern BS, 09-04-2024.
  • RBI raised risk weights on consumer credit on 16-11-2023. Governor Malhotra called the shift to equity a "healthy trend" BS, 06-08-2025.
  • RBI's Financial Stability Reports put household debt near 41–45% of GDP, low against EM peers; the five-year average itself was recomputed between reports.
Fact-check traps 6 items
  • Base change. All our ratios use the 2011-12 base. The 2022-23 base gives different levels and a different ending. Decision wait for DBIE, or use RBI's Annual Report tables as a named non-DBIE source.
  • 2022-23 net saving has at least three vintages (5.1%, 5.3%, 4.9%). Quote one, named.
  • HDFC's merger in July 2023 moves liabilities from HFCs to banks in 2023-24; the total is unaffected.
  • 2020-21 is a pandemic spike in net saving; use a pre-2019 baseline.
  • Physical savings still rest on the 2019 debt and investment survey; a new one runs to June 2027.
  • Gold and silver savings were revised up sharply in the new base; physical saving is not comparable across bases.

stories.title: Who lends to the government
stories.covers: Who holds the government's bonds, why banks hold them and what lenders earn.
stories.shows: G-sec ownership by holder since 2007; CRR and SLR history; 1- to 30-year yields since 1996
stories.oneLine: Banks once held half of the central government's bonds and now hold a third; savings pools and the RBI took up the rest. Now with reserve requirements and the yield curve.
stories.briefHtml:
Merged into S20 on 14-10-2026Wave 1Government and debtEffort: medium

Merged into S20. S20's lenders chapter now carries its ownership table, the reserve requirements and the yield curve; debt to GDP stays with S2 and lenders from abroad with S3. The plan below is kept for its research and traps.

In March 2007 banks held half of the central government's bonds. By March 2026 they held a third. Insurance companies held a steady quarter throughout, the RBI's share rose from 6.5% to 17.6%, and foreign investors, after three global index inclusions, hold 3%. Your LIC premium and PF contribution are part of this table.

49.7% → 33.0%
commercial banks' share of central government dated securities, Mar 2007 → Mar 2026 dated securities ownership
6.5% → 17.6%
RBI's share, same dates dated securities ownership
0.2% → 3.0%

Narrative

  1. Guess. "Who owns the most Indian government debt: banks, foreign investors, insurers or the RBI?" Most readers guess foreigners.
  2. 2007. Banks, half. Insurers, a quarter. Foreigners, almost none.
  3. The slow shift. Banks' share falls as their required bond holding (SLR) is cut to 18% by April 2020, and their holdings stay above it.
  4. The long-money holders. Insurers and provident and pension funds, with their need for long bonds; state bonds lean on provident funds.
  5. The RBI and the world. The RBI's share rises through bond purchases; foreign holdings rise with index inclusion but stay small. Close: public debt is mostly held by Indians' own savings.

For the reader

  • "Is India's debt mostly foreign?" answered: no, about 3%.
  • How their insurance and provident fund connect to the state's borrowing.
  • Shares and rupee amounts together: banks hold a smaller share of a much bigger total.

For economists

  • Central and state securities side by side; Treasury bills as a third panel.
  • Category-break markers and an "as reported" against "harmonised" toggle.
  • The financial-repression literature, attributed LEAP, 24-08-2024.
  • RBI holdings explained as liquidity operations, with the caveat that the table cannot say what share of the deficit RBI "financed".

Where readers play

Live debates

  • JP Morgan's index phased India in from 28-06-2024 to 10%; inflows fell short of the $20–30 billion projected BS. Bloomberg followed in January 2025 and FTSE from September 2025.
  • An ordinance of 05-06-2026 exempts foreign investors' interest and gains on government bonds AIR.
  • RBI's December 2025 FSR notes weaker long-bond demand from insurers and pension funds BS.
Fact-check traps 5 items
  • Pension funds were split out of "Others" from March 2022; the format was revised from the June 2023 Bulletin.
  • From September 2023 the banks' share includes the HDFC merger: part of the jump is a reclassification.
  • Central dated securities include special securities and Sovereign Gold Bonds; bank primary dealers sit with banks.
  • Recent quarters are provisional. Check that ₹125.7 lakh crore comes from the same table vintage as the shares.
  • Repo collateral is not outright holding. Do not say "RBI financed X% of the deficit" from these shares.
Added 14-10-2026: why banks hold bonds, and what lenders earn 2 chapters

Two candidates from the 14-10-2026 research join this story rather than stand alone. The rule: from September 1990 to January 1993 banks had to keep ₹15 of every ₹100 deposited with the RBI (CRR) and hold ₹38.50 in government bonds (SLR), ₹53.50 in all; since 29-11-2025 it is ₹21 (3% and 18%) Handbook 151 (.xlsx). The price: the ten-year government bond yield was 13.96% in May 1996, 5.11% in October 2003 and 6.96% in August 2026; in 21 months a one-year loan to the government paid more than a ten-year one; today the curve runs from 5.88% at one year to 7.51% at thirty Handbook 217.

  • The policy-rate CSVs are empty in the mirror; the values are only in the .xlsx.
  • 1996–98 yields step evenly, as if interpolated; label them estimated. Nothing beyond ten years before 2002.
  • Repo history and MPC votes (61 decisions since 04-10-2016, 37 unanimous) stay out unless Q24 says otherwise.

stories.briefHtml:
Wave 2StatesEffort: large

Income per person rose in every large state between 2011-12 and 2023-24. Gujarat's income per person more than doubled; Bihar's grew by half. So the ratio between them went from four to six. Bihar today is below where Gujarat was in 2011-12.

4.0 → 6.1
Gujarat ÷ Bihar per-capita income, 2011-12 → 2023-24, constant prices per-capita NSDP
×2.24
Gujarat, ₹87,481 → ₹1,95,617 per-capita NSDP
×1.48
Bihar, ₹21,750 → ₹32,227 per-capita NSDP
×2.05
Odisha, one of the lower-income states that grew fastest per-capita NSDP

Narrative

  1. Draw it. Readers draw how they think the gap between the highest- and lowest-income large states moved since 2012.
  2. Everyone rose. All 18 large states grew in real terms.
  3. The spread. The ratio widened: states with higher incomes in 2011-12 mostly grew faster.
  4. Exceptions. Odisha's income per person rose 2.05 times; West Bengal and Punjab moved down the ranking.
  5. Years behind. The time-distance view, and what ₹1 lakh means in each state.

For the reader

  • "Where does my state rank, and is it catching up?"
  • Gap shown in rupees and as a ratio, side by side.

For economists

  • σ-convergence (spread over time) and β-convergence (do poorer states grow faster), both computed and shown.
  • Ratio against absolute-gap toggle.
  • NSDP is production in the state, not residents' income; remittances to poorer states are not counted.

Where readers play

Pick your stateRatio / gapDraw-it guessTime-distance (guided)
Live debates
  • EAC-PM: Bihar's per-capita income fell from 70.3% of the national average in 1960-61 to 32.8% in 2023-24; Gujarat 160.7% EAC-PM, Sep 2024.
  • Absolute convergence is largely absent in the literature; some studies find conditional convergence Cherodian & Thirlwall.
  • The 16th Finance Commission keeps the states' share at 41% and changes the weights (secondary; verify from the report).
Fact-check traps 4 items
  • State accounts move to the 2022-23 base during 2026-27; our 2011-12 constant series will be superseded. Decision publish on the 2011-12 base, frozen and labelled, or wait.
  • Population denominators for recent years are projections; there has been no census since 2011.
  • States publish on different timetables; 2023-24 may be a quick estimate for some.
  • A wider ratio does not mean the poorer state shrank. Say both.
Added 14-10-2026: what living costs, state by state 1 chapter

Between 2013 and 2025 consumer prices rose 77% across India, 60% in Delhi and 93% in Kerala and Tripura; food rose 62% in Chhattisgarh and 117% in Manipur CPI state-wise, base 2012. A cost-of-living chapter beside the income gap: "a ₹1,000 basket in 2013 costs ₹X in your state".

  • Only rises compare across states, never index levels; no state price levels exist in DBIE.
  • The 2012-base series starts January 2013; CPI moved to a 2024 base from January 2026, and the mirror ends December 2025.

stories.overlaps: S11 has the gold-against-deposit race (S18 keeps gold to one chapter); S31 the unclaimed savings accounts; S24 homes as physical saving.

stories.briefHtml:
Owner: GeetikaWave 1Savings and marketsEffort: largeAdded 14-10-2026

What households save and borrow, where they keep their savings, and what each place earned. On the 2022-23 base households saved ₹69.0 lakh crore in 2024-25, ₹64.10 of every ₹100 of it in physical assets such as homes and gold. Households held ₹490 lakh crore in financial assets in March 2026: ₹34.40 of every ₹100 in bank deposits, ₹18.10 in shares, ₹15.70 in life insurance, ₹10.50 in mutual funds, ₹7.90 as cash, and the rest in small savings, pension funds and PPF. A fixed deposit renewed since 1971 is worth ₹130 today for every ₹100 put in; since 1990-91 the Sensex rose 7.7 times after prices. Mutual funds held ₹9 for every ₹100 in bank deposits in 2004, and ₹28 in 2026.

₹34 / ₹18 / ₹16
bank deposits, shares and life insurance per ₹100 of household financial assets, March 2026 household financial assets (Bulletin 1226)
₹9 → ₹28
mutual fund assets per ₹100 of bank deposits, Mar 2004 → Mar 2026 Handbook 126, 813
₹20.5lakh cr
small savings outstanding, March 2025; ₹52,874 crore in 1991 small savings
₹21.30
of every ₹100 households added to financial assets in 2024-25 went to provident and pension funds Handbook 246

Chapters

  1. The household's ₹100. The March 2026 mix above, with a guess first ("how much of a household's financial savings sits in bank deposits?"). The mix moves: life insurance took ₹17.30 of each ₹100 added in 2018-19 and ₹13.10 in 2025-26.
  2. Saving and borrowing. Folded in from S12 (What households keep). On the 2011-12 base, households' gross financial saving held at about 11–12% of GDP while borrowing rose from 3.8% of GDP in 2021-22 to 6.2% in 2023-24. On the 2022-23 base (Handbook 245), household saving was ₹69.0 lakh crore in 2024-25: gross financial saving ₹38.3 lakh crore and physical saving ₹44.3 lakh crore; physical assets were 70.3% of household saving in 2022-23 and 64.1% in 2024-25. The old and new bases are shown side by side, never spliced.
  3. The fixed deposit since 1971. ₹100 renewed each April becomes ₹6,710; prices rose 51.6 times, so it is worth ₹130. Its rate was below CPI-IW inflation in 19 of 55 years (2009-10: 6.5% against 12.4%). Who holds them: 28.0 crore term-deposit accounts; 72% are for one to three years; people aged 60 and over hold 49.4% of individuals' term deposits. Accounts under ₹1 lakh are 46.9% of accounts and 3.2% of the money.
  4. Small savings. Post office deposits, certificates and PPF: ₹9,774 crore outstanding in 1982, ₹20.5 lakh crore in 2025, now 70% deposits. By scheme (end-March 2025 as labelled): post office time deposits ₹3.06 lakh crore, monthly income scheme ₹2.69 lakh crore, Kisan Vikas Patra ₹2.21 lakh crore, senior citizens' scheme ₹1.75 lakh crore, Sukanya Samriddhi ₹1.58 lakh crore. Rates: PPF 8.1% in April 2016, 7.1% since April 2020; senior citizens' scheme 8.6% → 7.4% → 8.2%. PPF's margin over CPI-IW inflation ranged from 0.5 points (2019-20) to 4.0 points (2025-26).
  5. Provident and pension funds. They took ₹20.40 of every ₹100 households added to financial assets in 1971-72, ₹10.30 in 2011-12 and ₹21.30 in 2024-25 (₹8.17 lakh crore). Pension funds held ₹16.5 lakh crore and PPF ₹12.6 lakh crore in March 2026. Where the money goes: provident funds own ₹23.11 of every ₹100 of state government bonds (links to S13).
  6. Insurance. Life insurance funds are ₹77.2 lakh crore of household assets. LIC's investments grew from ₹4,588 crore in 1979 to ₹50.7 lakh crore in 2026, 79% in public-sector instruments; insurers hold ₹25.59 of every ₹100 of central government bonds.
  7. Markets. BSE companies were worth 4% of GDP in 1980 and 115% in 2026; the Sensex rose ×78 between 1990-91 and 2025-26, ×7.7 after prices before dividends, against ×1.45 for a fixed deposit. Mutual funds against deposits: ₹9 → ₹28 per ₹100.
  8. Gold. On the new 2022-23 base, households saved ₹2.18 lakh crore in gold and silver ornaments in 2024-25, ₹3.20 of every ₹100 of household saving. Close on "your year": ₹100 from any start year in a deposit, PPF, the Sensex and gold (from S11), set against prices.

Visual. A ₹100 household purse that re-sorts into deposits, shares, insurance, funds, cash, small savings and pensions; then jars for deposits and mutual funds filling from 1997; then ₹100 carried from the reader's chosen year. S12's household ledger (₹100 saved, borrowed back, kept) opens the story as the saving-and-borrowing chapter.

Pick a start yearDeposit / PPF / Sensex / gold against pricesYour household's ₹100After 30% tax (illustrative)
Fact-check traps 9 items
  • The household asset mix (Bulletin 1226) is an RBI compilation, not the NSO 2022-23 base; instruments join in steps (PPF, pension and small savings from March 2021, equity from June 2022), and its GDP note is stale. Quote the latest quarter's mix only, named.
  • Deposit rate: HB/282, end-March ranges of five major banks, midpoint applied to the whole year; rates before 1992 administered; 2026-27 row is part-year.
  • Small savings receipts fall from ₹4.34 lakh crore (2016-17) to ₹0.73 lakh crore (2017-18), apparently a gross-to-net change (unverified): no line across it. HB/746's scheme column may be a year behind its "end-March 2025" label; HB/231's PPF may be post-office PPF only.
  • Small savings rates are set by date, not quarterly; only change dates are in HB/746.
  • DBIE has no EPFO or NPS series (no subscribers, assets or contributions), no insurance premiums, no Sovereign Gold Bond or Gold Monetisation Scheme series. Say so; do not borrow them from elsewhere for headline numbers.
  • NSO (HB/246) and RBI (Bulletin 1225) estimates of provident and pension flows differ for 2024-25 (₹8.17 against ₹7.88 lakh crore); quote one, named. HB/246 states no base year.
  • Gold in household saving was revised up about 2.6 times on the 2022-23 base; never splice the two bases.
  • Term-deposit size: insurance cover is per depositor, not per account, so large accounts are not "uninsured". The size table changes format in March 2026.
  • Saving and borrowing: the 2011-12 base ends 2023-24 and the 2022-23 base (HB/245) starts 2022-23, with different levels; 2022-23 net financial saving has at least three vintages (5.1%, 5.3%, 4.9% of GDP). HB/245 gives totals only, not the instrument split; the HDFC merger moves household liabilities from HFCs to banks in 2023-24 without changing the total.
  • History, never advice: no "better", "should" or "safe".

stories.title: Services exports now earn 94% of what goods exports earn

stories.briefHtml:
Wave 1TradeEffort: largeAdded 14-10-2026

What India sells, what it buys, and to whom. In 1990-91 services earned a quarter of what goods exports did; in 2025-26, 94%. The partners changed: China went from 0.1% of imports to 15.7%. The goods gap stopped being about oil: non-oil goods were 64% of it in 2025-26. And the reserves that pay for imports went from 2.5 months' worth to 10.6.

25% → 94%
services exports as a share of goods exports, 1990-91 → 2025-26 balance of payments, annual
0.1% → 15.7%
China's share of India's imports, 1990-91 → 2024-25 direction of foreign trade
93% → 36%
oil's share of the goods trade gap, 1990-91 → 2025-26 foreign trade, oil and non-oil
2.5 → 10.6months
import cover of reserves, 1990-91 → 2025-26 BoP indicators

Chapters

  1. Services reach 94% of goods. $4.6 bn against $18.5 bn in 1990-91; $421.3 bn against $446.2 bn in 2025-26. Software appears as its own line at $6.3 bn in 2000-01 and reaches $203.7 bn. In four months since September 2025 services out-earned goods.
  2. The partners. The USSR took 16.1% of exports in 1990-91; Russia takes 1.1% now, but supplied 8.8% of imports in 2024-25 (1.4% in 2020-21). China supplies 15.7% of imports and takes 3.3% of exports. The USA takes 19.8% of exports.
  3. Oil, then everything else. Oil was 41.9% of imports in 1980-81 and 22.4% in 2025-26. Of the $333.2 bn goods gap in 2025-26, $213.1 bn was non-oil.
  4. Phones and chips. Electronics exports went from $5.6 bn (2009-10) to $38.6 bn (2024-25), more than gems and jewellery ($29.8 bn); electronics imports were $98.7 bn, second only to petroleum ($185.8 bn).
  5. The balance and the buffer. The $216.6 bn services surplus covered 64% of the goods gap. Reserves covered 2.5 months of imports in 1990-91 (foreign currency assets were $1.12 bn in June 1991, about 17 days of goods imports by our arithmetic), 17.4 months in 2020-21 and 10.6 in 2025-26.

Visual. Two lines, goods and services exports, from 1990-91 to 2025-26; a partner table that re-sorts year by year; the goods gap as a stacked oil and non-oil bar; a closing calendar strip filled with the months of imports the reserves could pay for. Gold stays with "The 10-gram question", external debt with "The long walk back from 1991".

Scrub 1990-91 → 2025-26Pick a partner countryPick an export itemSoftware / all services
Fact-check traps 7 items
  • Annual BoP: sdmx/external-sector/international-trade/indias-overall-balance-of-payments-annually.csv, BPM5 layout carried forward; BPM6 detail starts 2011-12. 2025-26 is preliminary.
  • The monthly SDMX goods file repeats rows from July 2025; deduplicate. April 2020's crossover is a lockdown month; leave it out.
  • "Russia" before 1991-92 is the USSR (unverified); country groupings change; direction data ends 2024-25.
  • In indias-foreign-trade-oil-non-oil-annually.csv the oil/non-oil codes are mislabelled; from the sums, plain = imports, "1" = exports, "2" = balance. Confirm against HB/149.
  • Commodity data: old series to 2013-14 and new from 2009-10, with different items; splice only on the overlap.
  • The 17-day figure is our arithmetic, not RBI's; gold was revalued in October 1990; TERM_IMP_RES is mislabelled in the mirror (it is months of cover); 2025-26 cover is in HB/178.
  • A deficit with a country is arithmetic, not a judgement; no dependence language.

Wave 1Government and debtEffort: mediumAdded 14-10-2026

Where the central government's money comes from and where it goes. Interest took ₹18 of every ₹100 of the centre's revenue in 1970-71, ₹53 in 2001-02 and ₹38 in 2025-26. Capital outlay rose from 6.7% of the centre's spending in 1998-99 to 18.4% in 2024-25. Direct taxes rose from 16.3% of all tax revenue in 1990-91 to 42.1%. Small savings provided ₹21.80 of every ₹100 of the centre's capital receipts in 2025-26.

₹18 → ₹53 → ₹38
interest per ₹100 of the centre's revenue receipts, 1970-71 → 2001-02 → 2025-26 RE Handbook 75, 181
6.7% → 18.4%
capital outlay as a share of the centre's spending, 1998-99 → 2024-25 Handbook 75
16.3% → 42.1%
direct taxes in combined centre and state tax revenue, 1990-91 → 2025-26 BE direct and indirect taxes
₹21.80
small savings (net) per ₹100 of the centre's capital receipts, 2025-26 (₹25.70 in 2020-21) central government receipts

Chapters

  1. The centre's ₹100 in. 2025-26 RE: net tax ₹54.4, non-tax ₹13.6, borrowing and other capital receipts ₹32.1.
  2. The centre's ₹100 out. Interest ₹25.7, capital outlay ₹17.9, defence ₹11.4, subsidies ₹9.5.
  3. Who pays the taxes. Direct taxes 16.3% → 42.1% of all tax revenue; personal income tax ₹8.15 lakh crore and corporation tax ₹6.95 lakh crore in 2025-26 RE, net of states' share.
  4. Savers lending to the centre. Net small-savings receipts were ₹52,465 crore in 2015-16, ₹4.84 lakh crore in 2020-21 and ₹3.43 lakh crore in 2025-26. Links to S18.
  5. Who lends to the centre. Folded in from S13 (Who lends to the government). Commercial banks held 49.7% of central government dated securities in March 2007 and 33.0% in March 2026; insurers about a quarter throughout; the RBI 6.5% → 17.6%; foreign portfolio investors 0.2% → 3.0%; provident funds hold 23% of state government bonds. Banks once had to keep ₹53.50 of every ₹100 deposited as cash with the RBI or in government bonds (1990–93); since November 2025 it is ₹21. The ten-year yield was 13.96% in May 1996 and 6.96% in August 2026. Debt to GDP is told in "The long walk back from 1991"; lenders from abroad in "From aid recipient to market borrower"; the states' half in S27.

Visual. A ₹100 note cut twice, "comes from" and "goes to", re-slicing as the years scrub, with interest highlighted; readers compare any two years.

Pick a yearCompare two yearsInterest slice (guided)
Fact-check traps 6 items
  • SDMX central-government-expenditures.csv is a vintage behind central-government-receipts.csv for its last two years; use HB/75 and HB/181, which flag RE and BE. SDMX receipts carry no BE/RE flag; 2025-26 small savings is probably RE (unverified).
  • One-offs to footnote: 2007-08 spending includes ₹35,531 crore for RBI's stake in SBI; 2010-11 receipts include the 3G auction (inferred); 2002-05 capital spending includes repayments to the NSSF.
  • The centre's liability line "small savings, deposits and provident funds" falls from ₹11.6 lakh crore (2019-20) to ₹5.7 lakh crore (2025-26), apparently a reclassification (unverified); do not draw a line across it.
  • DBIE carries no pension line for the centre; HB/75 shows defence, interest and subsidies only.
  • Tax figures net of states' share; RE and BE labelled every time.
  • Lenders chapter (from S13): pension funds split from "Others" in March 2022; banks' share includes the HDFC merger from September 2023; central securities include special securities and Sovereign Gold Bonds; the policy-rate CSVs are empty in the mirror (values in the .xlsx); 1996–98 yields look interpolated. Describes RBI's own operations: courtesy review (Q2).
  • Describe, never grade.

Wave 1CompaniesEffort: largeAdded 14-10-2026

Who gets each ₹100 that Indian companies earn, told three ways: listed companies' sales, factories' value added, and foreign-owned companies by the investor's country. Listed companies' interest bill halved as a share of sales in nine years. In registered factories, profit's share of each ₹100 of value added rose from ₹22.10 in 1990-91 to ₹51.00 in 2023-24, and workers' wages' share fell from ₹25.60 to ₹16.00.

₹4.90 → ₹2.40
interest per ₹100 of listed companies' sales, quarters to Jun 2016 → Dec 2025 listed companies, quarterly ratios
₹7.09 / ₹7.17lakh cr
listed companies' net profit and staff cost, 2024-25 listed companies, annual
₹25.60 → ₹16.00
workers' wages per ₹100 of factory value added, 1990-91 → 2023-24 Annual Survey of Industries
₹51.70 / ₹5.80
staff pay per ₹100 of spending, US- and Japanese-owned companies in India, 2024-25 FDI companies, country-wise

Chapters

  1. Listed companies' ₹100 of sales. Interest ₹4.90 → ₹2.40; interest cover 2.0 times in the lockdown quarter (June 2020) → 6.1 times (December 2025); net profit ₹6.70 (June 2014) → ₹9.40 (December 2025), against staff cost ₹8.00 → ₹10.50.
  2. Less borrowing. Public limited companies' debt to equity fell from 46.5% (2018-19) to 29.8% (2024-25).
  3. Factories. Registered factories grew from 1.1 lakh to 2.6 lakh and their workers from 63 lakh to 1.55 crore, 1990-91 → 2023-24. Of each ₹100 of net value added: wages ₹25.60 → ₹16.00, interest ₹28.90 → ₹10.60, profit ₹22.10 → ₹51.00. A worker's wage rose about 1.1 times after prices in 33 years.
  4. Foreign-owned companies. US-owned firms spend ₹51.70 of every ₹100 on staff, Japanese-owned ₹5.80; Japanese-owned firms kept 74% of 2024-25 profit, UK-owned 22%. Singapore is the investor of record for 802 companies, the US for 416.
  5. Private limited companies. Staff took ₹18.10 of every ₹100 of private limited companies' spending, against ₹9.90 at public limited companies; debt to equity 48.0% against 32.8%.
  6. How companies raise money. Private placements raised ₹13,361 crore in 1995-96 and ₹14.62 lakh crore in 2025-26 (12,012 issues); public equity issues by non-government companies ₹38,517 crore in 2022-23 and ₹1.89 lakh crore in 2025-26. Commercial paper outstanding ₹1.23 lakh crore (June 2011) and ₹5.27 lakh crore (April 2026).

Visual. One ₹100 note, sliced into raw materials, staff, interest, tax and profit, carried through three scenes: a listed company quarter by quarter from 2014, a factory year by year from 1990-91, and side-by-side country cards for foreign-owned firms. Readers pick an industry from the industry-wise files. The first story under a Companies heading.

Scrub quarters / yearsPick an industryPer ₹100 / per workerCountry cards
Fact-check traps 6 items
  • The listed-company sample changes every quarter (2,536 to 3,188) and jumps from 3,281 to 3,902 in 2024-25. Compare ratios, never levels across years. Say "listed private non-financial companies" every time.
  • Tax provision to pre-tax profit fell from about 24–25% to about 20% after 2019; state without a cause.
  • ASI coverage breaks: factories jump between 2009-10 and 2010-11; workers drop in 1998-99. Causes unverified; mark on the chart. Several ASI rupee items are labelled as pure numbers in the mirror.
  • Real factory wages: show both CPI-IW links (×1.14 by overlap years, ×1.08 with the official factors). Use shares, never real value added deflated by a consumer index.
  • Foreign-owned companies: "country" is the investor of record; Mauritius and Singapore are routing jurisdictions. Annual study, changing sample, no 2019-20 study year.
  • No claim about why shares moved; the wage-share fall is stated as arithmetic.
  • Private placements (table 398) include public sector issuers and widen in 2019-20 to add QIPs and preferential allotments; public issues (HB/261) cover a different set. Never compare them as a multiple. The latest private limited company ratios carry REF_TIME_RN=PREV_YR; confirm the accounts year.

Wave 1Bank creditEffort: mediumAdded 14-10-2026

Where India's banks are, where the money they collect comes from and where it is lent. There is one bank branch for every 8,425 people, against one for 62,697 in 1969. Banks lend ₹81.4 of every ₹100 deposited, the highest since 1951. Metropolitan areas hold 53% of deposits and get 58% of credit; central, eastern and north-eastern India hold 26% of deposits and get 18% of credit. The five largest states' share of credit fell from 65% in 2004 to 58% in 2026.

₹62 → ₹53 → ₹81
credit per ₹100 of deposits, all banks, 1950-51 → 2000-01 → 2025-26 SCB select aggregates (HB/813)
62,697 → 8,425
people per bank branch, 1969 → 2026 Our reading
53% / 58%
metropolitan areas' share of deposits and of credit, March 2026 (19% of offices) spatial distribution (1427)
64.8% → 58.5%
share of national credit in the five largest states, March 2004 → March 2026 spatial distribution (1483, 1427)

Chapters

  1. Branches reach people. 8,262 branches in 1969 (one for 62,697 people), 60,220 in 1991, 1,68,624 in 2026 (one for 8,425). Rural branches were 22.2% of the total in 1969, 58.5% in 1991 and 33.9% in 2026.
  2. The national ratio. Credit per ₹100 of deposits: ₹62.0 (1950-51), ₹79.3 (1970-71), ₹60.4 (1990-91), ₹51.7 at the 1998-99 low, ₹53.1 (2000-01), ₹75.7 (2010-11), ₹72.4 (2020-21), ₹81.4 (2025-26).
  3. Cities and villages. March 2026, by population group: metropolitan areas 53.2% of deposits and 58.1% of credit; rural areas 10.5% and 9.4%. Credit per ₹100 of deposits rose in every group between 2004 and 2026: rural ₹43.7 → ₹73.5, semi-urban ₹37.9 → ₹76.5, urban ₹47.3 → ₹70.8, metropolitan ₹75.7 → ₹89.4.
  4. Regions. Credit per ₹100 of deposits, 2004 → 2026: southern ₹68.1 → ₹96.4, western ₹72.0 → ₹95.6, northern ₹56.9 → ₹78.5, central ₹35.9 → ₹59.9, north-eastern ₹29.8 → ₹58.1, eastern ₹42.1 → ₹51.3. The southern and western regions hold 53.1% of deposits and get 62.3% of credit.
  5. Your state. The map: three states lend more than they collect in March 2026 (Andhra Pradesh ₹152, Tamil Nadu ₹121, Telangana ₹113), against one in 2004 (Chandigarh). The five largest states got 64.8% of credit in 2004 and 58.5% in 2026, while their share of deposits stayed at 54%.
  6. Beyond the large banks. Banks financed 255 self-help groups in 1992-93 and 53.5 lakh in 2025-26, lending ₹2.22 lakh crore. Regional rural banks' deposits were ₹232 crore in 1980-81 and ₹7.46 lakh crore in 2025-26; small finance banks' advances ₹7,173 crore (March 2017) and ₹3.38 lakh crore (March 2026).
  7. Deposit insurance. 97.4% of 301 crore accounts were fully covered in March 2026; insured deposits rose from ₹37.0 lakh crore (September 2019) to ₹76.2 lakh crore (September 2020) after cover rose from ₹1 lakh to ₹5 lakh on 04-02-2020. Depositors of 408 liquidated or merged banks have been paid ₹11,350 crore.

Visual. A map of branches spreading from 1969; then ₹100 deposited on one side and what was lent on the other, for India, then by population group and region; the state map comes last, as an interactive layer readers can switch between place of sanction and place of use.

India / region / population groupPick your stateSanction / useScrub 2004 → 2026
Fact-check traps 8 items
  • National ratio: HB/813 .xlsx (its CSV has years but no values). From 2023-24 it includes the HDFC merger: ex-merger 2024-25 is ₹79.14 against ₹80.79 reported, and 2025-26 has no ex-merger figure, so "highest since 1951" is stated as reported (the 1963-64 figure was ₹79.5).
  • Statement 3A files: 1483 and 1465 include regional rural banks; 1415 excludes them; 1427 (annual) includes them. Region, population-group and state comparisons use 1483 (2004) and 1427 (2026), both including RRBs. Andhra Pradesh ₹155 and Jharkhand ₹41 are the RRB-excluded file.
  • Place of sanction or of use: Statement 3A counts credit where it is sanctioned; HB/114 and BSR-1 table 1134 count it where it is used. ₹8.31 lakh crore sanctioned in Maharashtra is used in other states. Name the basis on every chart.
  • Census vintage: the 2001 and 2011 classifications overlap in 2016-17; about 3 points of the 2004 → 2026 shift towards metropolitan areas is reclassification.
  • People per branch uses mid-year population (HB/243); 2025-26 is provisional.
  • HB/115 changes source in 2006 (BSR to CISBI); rural and metropolitan branch counts step. HB/114's rural credit jumps in 1990 and 2005–2010.
  • Self-help group counts are labelled "in lakhs" but are plain counts; urban cooperative tables end 2023-24.
  • A map of facts, no ranking words; states and regions are compared, not graded.

stories.briefHtml:
Wave 1AgricultureEffort: mediumAdded 14-10-2026Absorbs S17

Farming in two halves: what the land produces, and what the grain is paid. Foodgrain output rose from 5.1 crore tonnes in 1950-51 to 35.8 crore in 2024-25, on 1.4 times the area. Wheat yields rose 5.4 times, pulses 2.1 times. The support price for paddy rose 1.76 times between 2013-14 and 2024-25, and farm workers' prices 1.73 times.

×7.04
foodgrain output, 50.8 → 357.7 million tonnes, 1950-51 → 2024-25 agricultural production
×5.4 / ×2.1
yield per hectare, wheat (663 → 3,595 kg) and pulses (441 → 926 kg) agricultural productivity
22.6 → 136.9m ha
gross irrigated area, same years land use and inputs
×1.76 / ×1.73
paddy MSP and CPI for agricultural labourers, 2013-14 → 2024-25 MSP CPI-AL

Chapters

  1. The same land. Net sown area 118.8 → 141.4 million hectares; foodgrain area 97.3 → 137.6.
  2. Water and fertiliser. Gross irrigated area ×6; fertiliser use from 69,000 to 3.29 crore tonnes.
  3. Yields by crop. Wheat ×5.4, rice ×4.4, pulses ×2.1; coffee 815 kg a hectare, as in 1970-71. Readers split any crop's growth into area and yield.
  4. From field to ration shop. The government procured 237.4 lakh tonnes of rice and wheat in 1990-91, 1,009.4 lakh tonnes in 2021-22 and 833.7 lakh tonnes in 2025-26; off-take 164.9, 1,058.0 and 675.2 lakh tonnes; stocks 158.1 and 943.9 lakh tonnes (1990-91 and 2025-26). Uttar Pradesh grew 37.0% of India's wheat in 1980-81 and 31.2% in 2022-23; Madhya Pradesh 21.4% in 2022-23.
  5. What the grain is paid. Folded in from S17 (Does MSP keep up?); it can follow in a second edition if its checks (crop-year alignment, cost benchmarks) take longer than the rest: support prices for paddy and wheat against farm workers' prices since 1997; quintals of wheat ₹1 lakh bought at MSP, 161 in 2001 and 39 in 2026.

Visual. One hectare drawn as a square that fills with sacks year by year, wheat and pulses side by side; then the sacks ₹1 lakh buys at MSP, fewer each year. Pairs with "The women who stayed" (who works the land) and S14 (what a day's farm wage buys).

Pick a cropArea / yield splitMSP deflator toggle
Fact-check traps 6 items
  • 2025-26 values are third advance estimates; end at 2024-25.
  • SDMX labels crop year 1950-51 as TIME_PERIOD 1951-03-31.
  • Pesticide consumption in the land-use file looks about 100 times too large; leave it out until checked.
  • Kharif and rabi marketing years are labelled differently; align MSP years against CACP tables.
  • CPI-AL rebased in June 2025; end the MSP comparison at 2024-25 or use an official linking factor.
  • MSP matters where procurement happens; say so without judging the policy. No claim about why yields rose.
  • In the procurement file RI, RIC and RICE are all labelled "Rice" (and likewise wheat): from the sums, procurement, off-take and stocks. 2020-23 off-take includes pandemic schemes; the 2026-27 row is part-year; early stock units are implausible; state crop data end 2022-23.

stories.briefHtml:
Wave 2Real estateEffort: largeAdded 14-10-2026

A home is the largest purchase most families make. Banks' home loans reached ₹33.6 lakh crore in March 2026, rates came down from 10.71% in 2014 to 7.75%, and the average loan rose from ₹11.2 lakh to ₹21.7 lakh. Prices moved very differently by city: in Lucknow houses cost 4.2 times their 2010-11 price, in Kanpur, in the same state, 1.8 times. Consumer prices rose 2.3 times.

₹11.20 → ₹15.80
housing loans per ₹100 of non-food bank credit, Mar 2008 → Mar 2026 (₹33,55,963 crore) sectoral deployment of bank credit
×4.19 / ×1.81
house price index, Lucknow and Kanpur, 2010-11 → 2024-25; all ten cities ×3.23 house price index
10.71% → 7.75%
average rate on banks' housing loans, Mar 2014 → Jun 2026 BSR-1 WALR
₹11.2 → ₹21.7lakh
average housing credit limit, Mar 2017 → Jun 2026 BSR-1 size of credit limit

Chapters

  1. Ten cities, ten stories. RBI's house price index rose 3.23 times between 2010-11 and 2024-25. Lucknow ×4.19, Bengaluru ×3.66, Delhi ×3.49, Mumbai ×3.04; Kanpur ×1.81, Jaipur ×1.78. The highest city stood 1.31 times the lowest in 2011-12 and 2.36 times in 2024-25. Lucknow and Kanpur split in three years: by 2013-14 Lucknow was at 194 and Kanpur at 84; since then both rose 2.2 times.
  2. After prices. Against CPI-IW (×2.28), the ten-city index rose 1.42 times; Kanpur and Jaipur are below their 2010-11 level in real terms (0.79, 0.78). Delhi rose 4.5% from 2017-18 to 2024-25 while urban consumer prices rose 43%. Urban housing in the CPI, a rent measure, rose 1.67 times from 2013-14 against house prices' 1.89.
  3. The loan book. Housing credit went from ₹11.8 lakh crore (March 2019) to ₹33.6 lakh crore (March 2026). In July 2023 the merger of a housing finance company with a bank added ₹4.39 lakh crore in one step; excluding it, growth was 17.1% to March 2024, 10.7% to March 2025 and 11.5% to March 2026. Commercial real estate is a further ₹6.3 lakh crore.
  4. Bigger loans, cheaper money. Loans above ₹50 lakh are 13.4% of housing accounts and 45.6% of the amount (3.3% and 23.4% in 2017). The share of the amount lent below 8% went from 85.8% (March 2022) to 9.3% (June 2023) and back to 70.2% (June 2026). On a ₹50 lakh, 20-year loan at the average rate, the EMI is ₹41,047 now against ₹50,626 in 2014 Our reading.
  5. Loans by city. Home loans sanctioned in Lucknow district grew from ₹3,571 crore to ₹28,776 crore between March 2014 and March 2026 (×8.1, now 22% of the district's bank credit); Kanpur Nagar from ₹1,667 crore to ₹9,899 crore (×5.9). Jaipur's home loans grew 9.3 times while its price index rose the least of the ten cities, shown side by side, without a link drawn.
  6. Building it. Construction is 8.95% of real GVA in 2025-26 (2022-23 base). Cement output is 2.15 times its 2011-12 level while cement's wholesale price is 1.30 times; a rural mason's daily wage rose from ₹205 to ₹638 (2010-11 → 2024-25). Physical assets, homes among them, are 64.1% of household saving in 2024-25.

Visual. Ten city lines on the shared timeline scrubber, with a lens: "₹1 lakh of house in 2010-11 reads ₹4.19 lakh in Lucknow, ₹1.81 lakh in Kanpur" (a reading of the index, not a valuation), and a nominal or real toggle. Then a stack of ₹100 of bank credit in which the home-loan slice grows, the merger marked as a step. Then an EMI dial: pick a quarter from 2014 and see the payment on ₹50 lakh, with the rate bands behind it. The Lucknow and Kanpur pair returns at the end with district loans beside prices.

Pick a cityNominal / realEMI by quarterLoan-size bands
Fact-check traps 8 items
  • House price index: sdmx/real-sector/prices-wages/house-price-index.csv, 2010-11 base, ten cities, ends with the quarter to 31-03-2025; the 2008-09 base (nine cities) is separate. Whether RBI has replaced it is unverified; if so, the city chapter waits. A duplicate 2020-08-31 period must be dropped.
  • It is an index from registration data: transaction prices, never ₹ per square foot or a "value of your home". No advice about buying.
  • Use CPI-IW ×2.28 (official linking factor 2.88), not the ×2.22 that overlap chaining gives.
  • HDFC merger: from 28-07-2023 housing credit includes it; ex-merger figures in parentheses run only to June 2025 (file 540's footnote). Mark the step, quote ex-merger growth, and never compare levels across it. The same break shows in BSR-1 accounts and household liabilities to HFCs.
  • Sectoral credit has an old format (2008–2020) and a new one (from January 2019) that disagree for March 2019; no splice without a note. Sectoral data cover about 95% of banks, non-food credit all banks, so the ₹15.80 share is approximate. Reporting moved to month-end from 31-12-2025.
  • BSR-1 WALR is on outstanding loans, not new loans; the EMIs are illustrations. District data are by district of sanction and include RRBs.
  • Construction share uses the 2022-23 GDP base; the 2011-12 base is retired. Household physical saving is all physical assets, not homes alone.
  • Not in DBIE: ₹ prices or rents by city, sales, starts or inventory, housing finance companies' own loan books, construction jobs. Say so where a reader would expect them.

Wave 1BanksEffort: mediumAdded 14-10-2026

Eleven years of every bank group's loans, provisions, capital and earnings, quarter by quarter. Non-performing loans at public sector banks rose from ₹4.97 of every ₹100 lent in March 2015 to ₹14.58 in March 2018, then fell to ₹1.93 in March 2026. Their capital ratio rose from 11.45% to 16.59%. Industry's share of bank loans halved, from 44.4% to 22.2%, and retail loans' share rose from 18.5% to 33.4%.

₹4.97 → ₹14.58 → ₹1.93
public sector banks' gross NPAs per ₹100 of advances, Mar 2015 → Mar 2018 → Mar 2026 bank-group panels (1221)
11.45% → 16.59%
public sector banks' capital to risk-weighted assets, Mar 2015 → Mar 2026 bank-group panels (1221)
−0.87% → 1.10%
public sector banks' return on assets, Mar 2018 → Mar 2026 bank-group panels (1221)
44.4% → 22.2%
industry's share of all scheduled commercial banks' loans, Mar 2015 → Mar 2026 bank-group panels (1221)

Chapters

  1. Non-performing loans by bank group. Gross NPAs per ₹100 of advances, March 2015 → March 2018 → March 2026: public sector banks ₹4.97 → ₹14.58 → ₹1.93; private banks ₹2.10 → ₹4.62 → ₹1.47; foreign banks ₹3.20 → ₹3.81 → ₹0.56; all banks ₹4.28 → ₹11.18 → ₹1.73. The all-bank series from 1997 sets the long frame.
  2. Provisions. Public sector banks' provision coverage (write-off adjusted) went from 46.04% to 94.72%; their net NPAs from ₹7.97 per ₹100 (March 2018) to ₹0.39 (March 2026).
  3. Capital. Capital to risk-weighted assets: public sector banks 11.45% → 16.59%, all banks 12.94% → 17.68%, March 2015 → March 2026.
  4. Earnings. Public sector banks' return on assets −0.87% in 2017-18 and 1.10% in 2025-26; return on equity −14.01% and 14.82%. All banks' net interest margin 2.85% (2015) and 3.26% (2026).
  5. Who banks lend to, and who lends. The size of the economy, what it is made of, who works where, what is spent and who invests. GDP was ₹345.4 lakh crore in 2025-26, ₹2,43,107 a person. Agriculture's share of output fell from 53.2% in 1950-51 to 16.8%; rural men working in farming fell from 690 in every 1,000 in 2000-01 to 478 in 2025.   • DBIE does not say whether table 1005 includes balances already transferred to RBI's Depositor Education and Awareness Fund (from 2014, an outside fact); DBIE carries no DEA Fund series. Say "as reported", with no claim about where the money is held.
